opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been really interesting to watch. The first use cases tend to be pretty contained. A team comes in with a specific question they'd normally answer with a survey or a focus group: how will people react to this product concept, this message, this pricing change? Simulation is attractive because it's fast and cheap, and you can iterate on it in an afternoon instead of waiting weeks for a panel to come back.

Once they see the simulated responses actually track how real people behave, and that's always the critical moment, the ambition starts to expand in a couple of directions.

The first is going from a single question to an ongoing loop. They stop thinking of it as "let me run a survey" and start thinking of it as "let me have a population I can consult continuously." Every decision, every draft, every variation gets tested against it. That's a big mindset shift, because it changes simulation from a research tool into part of how the organization makes decisions day to day.

The second is going from individuals answering questions to people interacting with each other and with a system over time. That's where it gets really exciting for me, and it connects to the generative agents work. A lot of the questions people really care about aren't "what does one person think right now?" They're "what happens when this policy rolls out across a community?" or "how does an idea spread through a network?" or "how will behavior change six months after we launch this?" Those are emergent, social, dynamic questions, and they've historically been very hard to study because you can't easily run the experiment in the real world.

So the trajectory I see is roughly: start by replacing a survey, then replace a lot of the research pipeline, and eventually get to something like a sandbox for society, where you can ask counterfactual questions about groups of people before you make decisions that affect them.

I'd add one caveat, which is that the ambition has to be matched by rigor. The more consequential the decision, the more important it is to validate that the simulation reflects real human behavior, and to be honest about where it doesn't. That's a big part of what we focus on: grounding these agents in real people's data and measuring how faithfully they replicate them. The ambitions are growing quickly, and I think they should, but the trust has to be earned at each step.

r002.rationale: It discusses populations and communities, but does not identify testing ideas across thousands of subpopulations.

r003.rationale: It mentions behavior changing over time after launch, but does not describe simulated agents experiencing a product over time as product testing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so what we've seen is that almost everyone comes in the door with the same first ask, which is basically a faster, cheaper survey. They have a question they would normally take to a panel or a focus group, it would take them six weeks and a lot of money, and they want to know if they can get a reasonable read on it in an afternoon. And that's a totally legitimate starting point. Honestly, it's the right place to start, because it's the use case where you can actually check the answer. You can run the simulation and the real study side by side and see where they agree and where they don't.

But what's interesting is what happens after that first project. Once people trust the thing a little bit, the questions change shape. They stop asking "what would my customers say about this one feature," and they start asking things a survey could never really answer. Like, what happens if we change pricing and a competitor responds, and then our users talk to each other about it? Or, we have a policy we're thinking about rolling out, and we want to see how it plays out over months, not just what people say they'd do on day one. That's a very different kind of object. You're not simulating an opinion anymore, you're simulating a system of people who have memory, who react to each other, whose behavior drifts over time.

And I think that's the real arc. The first use case is replacing a measurement. The ambition that develops is something closer to having a rehearsal space for decisions. You get to run the thing a hundred times before you run it once in the world.

The thing I always try to push on, though, is that as the ambition grows, the validation problem grows with it. For a single survey question, we have ground truth, we can score ourselves. For a six-month dynamic with a thousand interacting agents, it gets much harder to say what "accurate" even means. So part of what I see maturing in the best customers is not just bigger ambitions, it's a more sophisticated sense of which questions a simulation can be trusted on, which ones it can only inform, and how to design studies where you can keep checking it against reality. The ones who get the most out of it are the ones who treat it as a scientific instrument with error bars, not as an oracle.

r003.rationale: It mentions behavior playing out over months, but not simulated agents experiencing a product over time as product testing.

astra-6.text:
I think people often start with a fairly specific question: “Can I test this product idea?” or “Can I understand how customers might respond to this message?” That’s a concrete place to begin because they already have a process for answering that question, and they can compare what the simulation tells them with what they learn from people.

As they build confidence, the ambition shifts from testing one thing to exploring a broader set of possibilities. Instead of asking, “Which of these two options works better?” they start asking, “What options haven’t we considered? How might different groups respond? And how could those responses change over time?”

That shift is exciting, but it also raises the bar for validation. Being useful for a narrow question doesn’t automatically mean a simulation can capture an entire market or community. So I think the ambition grows toward richer, more dynamic simulations, while the evidence has to grow alongside it.

Then the ambition starts to expand. Instead of asking how someone responds to one thing, they want to understand how that response changes over time, or how people influence each other. You move from testing a single interaction toward simulating a richer social environment.

The important thing is that the validation has to grow along with that ambition. Being useful for one narrow question doesn’t automatically mean a simulation can answer every question about human behavior.
